title: Implement Projection
aim: To implement the perspective projection of 3D points onto the image plane with the pinhole model x = K [R | t] X, to compare it with orthographic projection and with cv2.projectPoints, and to use projection for augmented-reality overlays on calibrated images and for planar homographies.
objectives: Project a 3D wireframe with $\mathbf{x} = K[R\,|\,t]\mathbf{X}$ in NumPy and verify the result against cv2.projectPoints.
Compare perspective with orthographic projection and estimate a pose with cv2.solvePnP for augmented reality.
Rectify a planar scene with a homography and synthesise a rotated view.
theory: In the pinhole model a point $(X_c, Y_c, Z_c)$ is divided by its depth. That division produces foreshortening and vanishing points. In homogeneous coordinates the projection is linear, $\mathbf{x} \sim K [R\,|\,t] \mathbf{X}$, and the camera centre is $C = -R^T t$.

Orthographic projection drops the depth, $u = s X_c + c_x$, $v = s Y_c + c_y$, so image size does not change with distance. The perspective-n-point problem (cv2.solvePnP) is the inverse: given known 3D points and their pixels it recovers $R$ and $t$. With that pose, a virtual object defined in the board frame can be projected into the photograph.
When the scene is a plane the projection reduces to a $3 \times 3$ homography $H$ with eight degrees of freedom, fixed by four correspondences. A pure camera rotation is also a homography.

$$\begin{bmatrix} u' \\ v' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} h_{11} & h_{12} & h_{13} \\ h_{21} & h_{22} & h_{23} \\ h_{31} & h_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad H_{\mathrm{rot}} = K R K^{-1}$$
tools: Python 3.11, OpenCV 5.0, NumPy, Matplotlib; intrinsic parameters loaded from outputs/exp02/calibration.npz
dataset: Synthetic 3D house wireframe (10 vertices, 17 edges); chessboard images left01, left03, left05 and left08 (640 x 480) and the sudoku.png photograph (558 x 563) from the OpenCV samples/data repository.
algorithm: Load $K$ from the calibration experiment and define the house vertices in metres.
Build $R = R_x(115^\circ) R_z(-35^\circ)$ and $t = (0, 0, d)^T - R\mathbf{X}_o$ for $d = 4$, 8 and 20 m.
Project the vertices in NumPy, scale $f$ by $d/6$ so the house keeps its image size, and compare with cv2.projectPoints.
Project the same pose orthographically and compare the front and back edge lengths of the house.
Solve the pose of four chessboard images with cv2.solvePnP and draw the board axes and a 75 mm cube.
Compute the homography from the sudoku corners to a $450 \times 450$ square and rectify the image with cv2.warpPerspective.
Map the $9 \times 9$ grid back with $H^{-1}$ and synthesise a 25 degree pan, 10 degree tilt view with $K R K^{-1}$.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1: Perspective projection of the house (NumPy lines, cv2.projectPoints dots) at camera distances of 4, 8 and 20 m.
Figure 3.2: The same pose under perspective (left) and orthographic (right) projection.
Figure 3.3: Board axes and a 75 mm cube projected onto four views with the pose from cv2.solvePnP.
Figure 3.4: Sudoku rectified by a homography, the grid mapped back with $H^{-1}$, and the view from a rotation-only homography.

results: NumPy projection and cv2.projectPoints agree to $8.5 \times 10^{-14}$ px. At $d = 4$ m the front edge of the house measures 250.0 px and the back edge 192.1 px, a ratio of 1.30. Under orthographic projection both edges are 229.0 px.

cv2.solvePnP returned $t = (-75.28, -108.94, 399.82)$ mm for left01.jpg, the same as the calibration extrinsics. The four board distances are 421, 336, 343 and 338 mm, and the cube sits on the board in every view.
conclusion: The hand-written projection matched OpenCV to machine precision, and foreshortening decreased with distance until the drawing approached the orthographic limit. A solvePnP pose placed a virtual cube on real photographs, and the homography rectified the sudoku grid and synthesised a rotated view.
